_comment: Forum corpus. Each thread is a conversation; the chunker pairs the opening question with ONE answer per chunk so competing answers can be ranked (and contradicted) independently. Vote counts and author roles drive the authority signal; is_accepted marks what the OP accepted, which is deliberately NOT always correct (see t_0007).

threads.title: Does timeout=0 disable the job timeout?

posts.author: dmitri_k
posts.body:
I have a long-running report job that keeps getting killed partway through. I want to let it run as long as it needs. Someone told me to set timeout=0 to turn the timeout off entirely. Is that right?

client.enqueue('reports', payload, timeout=0)

posts.author: marco_builds
posts.body: Yes, timeout=0 disables the timeout. Zero means no limit, same convention as most HTTP clients and socket libraries. I use timeout=0 on all my long transcode jobs and they run for 20+ minutes without being killed. Just set it and you are fine.

posts.author: jen_zephyr
posts.body:
This accepted answer is wrong and I want to correct it before it spreads further. timeout=0 does NOT disable the timeout in Zephyr. It means fail-fast: the attempt is abandoned immediately and the job fails on its first attempt, then retries per the retry policy.

If you genuinely want no per-attempt limit, omit timeout or pass timeout=None. For long jobs the better pattern is a generous timeout plus job.heartbeat() to extend the lease as you make progress.

If marco's transcode jobs are completing, they are completing on a retry after the first attempt fails instantly, which is not the behaviour he thinks he is getting.

posts.author: dmitri_k
posts.body: Confirmed. I checked attempt_count on my jobs and every single one shows attempt 2. The first attempt was failing instantly the whole time. timeout=None is what I actually wanted.

threads.title: Can I see the payload of a dead-lettered job from the CLI?

posts.author: sana_p
posts.body: zephyr dlq list gives me the job id, attempt count and error class, but not the payload. I need the payload to work out which records failed. Do I have to fetch each job through the SDK one at a time, or is there a CLI way?

posts.author: ravi_zephyr
posts.body:
There is an undocumented flag for exactly this:

zephyr dlq list --queue emails --include-payload

It adds a payload column, and with --json you get the full payload object per entry. It is not on the CLI reference page yet, which is an oversight on our side rather than a deliberate omission; I have filed a docs ticket.

Two caveats: payloads are truncated to 2 KiB in table output (use --json for the full object), and the flag increases response size substantially, so pair it with --limit when you are scanning a large DLQ.

zephyr dlq list --queue emails --include-payload --json --limit 20

posts.author: sana_p
posts.body: Works perfectly, thank you. Worth noting for anyone else that --include-payload does not appear in zephyr dlq list --help either, so there was no way to discover it.

threads.title: CLI will not start on Windows - credential_store_unreadable

posts.author: tom_h
posts.body:
Fresh install of zephyr-cli on Windows 11. Every command fails immediately:

$ zephyr queues list
Error: credential_store_unreadable

Same on two different Windows machines. Works fine on my Mac with an identical config. Is the CLI just broken on Windows? I am on 3.0.4.

posts.author: lena_ops
posts.body:
The CLI is broken on Windows in 3.0 - this is a known bug, not a config problem on your end. The credential store resolves ~/.config/zephyr/credentials through a symlink check that assumes POSIX symlink semantics, and it throws on Windows regardless of whether a symlink is involved. Every 3.0.x release is affected on every Windows host.

Workaround until you can upgrade: bypass the credential store entirely by setting the env var, which is read before the file is touched.

setx ZEPHYR_API_KEY zq_live_yourkey

Then open a new terminal. That got me unblocked for weeks.

posts.author: jen_zephyr
posts.body: Following up now that 3.1 has shipped: the symlink resolution bug is fixed, and Windows is a fully supported platform from 3.1 onward. pip install --upgrade zephyr-cli to pick it up. Anyone still pinned to 3.0.x will keep hitting this; the env var workaround lena described remains the only option on that version.

threads.title: Best way to enqueue in bulk from a cron script?

posts.author: priya_r
posts.body: I have a nightly script that needs to enqueue around 4000 jobs. What is the recommended call pattern so I do not hit the rate limit?

posts.author: oldtimer_jay
ravi_zephyr
posts.body:
Careful with that snippet - client.queue.push() is the pre-v3 API. It still works in 3.x but it is deprecated, emits a DeprecationWarning, and is scheduled for removal in 4.0. It also cannot take an idempotency_key, which you really want in a nightly cron that might get re-run.

The current call is client.enqueue(), and for bulk work use enqueue_many(), which sends up to 100 jobs as a single request and therefore costs one unit of rate-limit quota instead of 100:

for batch in chunked(items, 100):
    client.enqueue_many('nightly', batch)

4000 jobs becomes 40 requests, nowhere near the 600 rpm quota, and you can drop the sleep entirely.

threads.title: How long until dead-lettered jobs get retried?

posts.author: felix_m
posts.body: Some jobs went to the DLQ during a database outage last night. The outage is over. How long do I wait for them to be picked back up automatically?

posts.author: quickanswer_99
posts.body: I believe the DLQ sweeps and replays automatically about once an hour, so they should come back on their own. I would give it until the next hour boundary before doing anything manually.

posts.author: jen_zephyr
posts.body:
That is not correct, and waiting will not help - there is no automatic replay of any kind. No sweep, no timer, no hourly job. A dead-lettered job stays in the DLQ until you replay it or delete it, and it is deleted permanently after 30 days.

This is intentional: a job that already failed six times usually fails a seventh, and automatic replay would turn a broken handler into an unbounded loop.

For your outage case, bulk replay is what you want:

zephyr dlq replay-all --queue <q> --limit 500

Or client.dlq.replay_all(queue='...', limit=500). Fix the cause first, then replay - replaying into a still-broken dependency just refills the DLQ.

posts.author: carl_v
posts.body: Running zephyr-agent on a 32-core box. I expected 10 concurrent handlers based on what I read about defaults, but I am seeing 32 in flight at once. Is the default being ignored?

posts.author: ravi_zephyr
posts.body:
Nothing is being ignored - you are running a self-hosted agent, and agent concurrency defaults to the host CPU count, which is 32 on your box.

The figure of 10 you read applies to managed workers (zephyr worker start), which run on shared infrastructure where the visible CPU count tells you nothing useful about available capacity, so the default is a fixed number instead. Two different components, two different defaults.

If you want 10 on the agent, set it explicitly:

zephyr-agent start --queue emails --concurrency 10

threads.title: Jobs retry forever when the API returns 429

posts.author: hannah_t
posts.body:
During our evening peak the API starts returning 429 and then everything falls apart. Jobs retry in a tight loop, burn through all 5 attempts in well under a minute, and land in the DLQ.

The 429 responses clearly carry Retry-After: 30, so I expected the SDK to wait 30 seconds between attempts. Instead the gaps are about 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s. It behaves exactly as if Retry-After is not being read at all. Running SDK 3.0.7.

posts.author: lena_ops
posts.body:
You are not imagining it - the 3.0 SDK parses Retry-After and then discards it, falling back to plain exponential backoff. I packet-captured this to be sure.

The documented behaviour (honour Retry-After) is correct for 3.1+, but on 3.0 it is simply not implemented, so under sustained rate limiting your whole retry budget is spent inside the window the server asked you to wait out.

Upgrade to 3.1 or later and it behaves as documented. If you are stuck on 3.0, catch RateLimited and re-enqueue with an explicit delay instead of letting the automatic retry handle it:

except RateLimited as e:
    client.enqueue(q, payload, delay_seconds=e.retry_after)

posts.author: hannah_t
posts.body: Upgraded to 3.1.2 and the retry gaps now match Retry-After exactly. DLQ has been empty for two days through two peak windows that would previously have filled it.

threads.title: DLQ fills up during traffic spikes even though nothing is actually broken

posts.author: ben_oz
posts.body: Every marketing send pushes a few hundred jobs into the DLQ. last_error is RateLimited on all of them. The handler is fine - if I replay them afterwards they all succeed. It looks like the retries are not spacing themselves out during the spike.

posts.author: sana_p
posts.body:
Same thing bit us. On 3.0 the SDK does not respect Retry-After, so when you get a 429 asking you to wait 30s, it waits 1s, then 2s, then 4s, and the retry budget is gone before the rate-limit window closes. Independent of the handler being healthy.

3.1 fixed it for us - identical workload, DLQ stayed empty. Worth checking your exact SDK version, we thought we were on 3.1 and were actually pinned to 3.0.9 by a transitive dependency.

threads.title: Retry-After header seems to be ignored - is this expected?

posts.author: yuki_n
posts.body: The docs say the SDK honours Retry-After on 429 responses. I logged every attempt timestamp and the intervals are 1.0s, 1.9s, 4.1s, 8.0s regardless of what Retry-After says - I have seen it set to 12 and to 45 and the intervals do not change. Is the documentation describing intended behaviour rather than shipped behaviour?

posts.author: jen_zephyr
posts.body: Your reading is right and the docs were ahead of the implementation for 3.0. The header was parsed but never applied to scheduling. It is fixed in 3.1, released last week, and the reference page describes 3.1+ behaviour. Apologies for the confusion - we should have version-gated that paragraph. Upgrade to 3.1.0 or later and the intervals will track Retry-After.

threads.title: 413 payload_too_large but my payload looks small

posts.author: nadia_s
posts.body: Getting 413 payload_too_large with received_bytes 491020. But the dict I am passing has maybe 40 keys. What is inflating it?

posts.author: lena_ops
posts.body:
Almost always base64. If any of those 40 keys holds a file, an image or a PDF, base64 adds about 33% on top of the raw bytes and you blow past the 256 KiB limit fast.

Check the real serialised size rather than eyeballing the dict:

len(json.dumps(payload).encode('utf-8'))

The fix is the claim-check pattern - put the blob in object storage and enqueue the key instead of the bytes. Smaller payloads, cheaper retries, and you stop re-sending the blob on every attempt.

threads.title: Same job running twice - idempotency key not working?

posts.author: omar_f
posts.body: I pass an idempotency_key on every enqueue and I am still seeing charge handlers run twice for the same invoice. Is the key broken?

posts.author: ravi_zephyr
posts.body:
The key is working; it is solving a different problem than the one you have. idempotency_key deduplicates ENQUEUES - two enqueues with the same key create one job. It does not deduplicate DELIVERIES.

Zephyr is at-least-once, so one job can be delivered more than once: worker dies before acking, handler outruns the visibility timeout, network partition hides the ack. All three redeliver. So the handler itself has to be idempotent.

Check your visibility timeout first - handler runtime exceeding the 30s default is by far the most common cause of exactly this symptom. Then write a completion marker in the same transaction as the side effect.

posts.author: omar_f
posts.body: That was it - the charge call takes about 35 seconds against our payment provider and the visibility timeout was the default 30. Raised it to 180 and added a marker row in the same transaction. No duplicates since.

posts.author: gus_w
posts.body: Upgraded from 2.4 to 3.0 and now every single request is 401. The key is valid - it works from the old service that has not been upgraded yet. I regenerated it twice. What changed?

posts.author: lena_ops
posts.body:
The auth header changed in 3.0. Authorization: Zephyr <key> was removed; it is X-Zephyr-Key: <key> now.

The error code gives it away if you look at the body rather than the status - unauthorized_header_form rather than revoked_api_key. Regenerating the key will never fix it.

If you are hand-rolling requests, change the header. If you are on the SDK, it handles this for you, so a 401 there means something is still sending the old header - usually a cached layer or a sidecar.

threads.title: What is the maximum number of jobs per enqueue_many call?

posts.author: ling_z
posts.body: Is there a documented cap on enqueue_many batch size? I am passing 500 at a time and getting errors.

posts.author: jen_zephyr
posts.body:
100 per call. Over that you get invalid_batch_size and nothing is enqueued - it is not a partial accept.

The whole batch counts as a single request against the 600 rpm quota regardless of how many jobs it holds, which is why batching is the best lever for staying inside the quota. Chunk your 500 into five calls of 100.

threads.title: How do I check why a specific job failed?

posts.author: ivan_d
posts.body: A job failed and I have the job id from our logs. What is the fastest way to see what went wrong?

posts.author: lena_ops
posts.body:
job = client.get_job('job_8f2a91c4') then look at job.status, job.attempt_count and job.last_error. last_error holds the exception class and message from the final attempt.

If attempt_count is higher than you expected, the job was redelivered rather than retried - check the visibility timeout against your handler runtime.

From the CLI, zephyr dlq list --queue <q> --json gives you the same fields for everything that dead-lettered.

threads.title: Jobs being picked up by two workers at once

posts.author: rosa_b
posts.body: Two different workers log the same job id within a minute of each other. I thought a claimed job was invisible to other workers. Is this a bug?

posts.author: ravi_zephyr
posts.body:
It is invisible, but only for the visibility timeout - 30 seconds by default since v3.0. If your handler has not acknowledged within that window the job becomes visible again and another worker legitimately claims it. So a handler that takes 45 seconds will always be double-executed on the default setting.

Two fixes, use both: raise the visibility timeout above your realistic worst case (client.update_queue('q', visibility_timeout=300)), and call job.heartbeat() periodically inside long handlers to extend the lease as you progress.

Note the default used to be 60s in 2.x and dropped to 30s in 3.0, which catches a lot of people mid-upgrade - handlers that were fine for years suddenly double-run.

threads.title: Job disappeared without reaching the DLQ

posts.author: pedro_l
posts.body: We paused our workers for about ten days during a migration. Some jobs enqueued before the pause are simply gone - not completed, not in the DLQ. Where did they go?

posts.author: jen_zephyr
posts.body:
Pending jobs have a 7-day TTL. A job that is still pending when its TTL expires is routed to the DLQ with error class TTLExpired - and DLQ entries are themselves retained for 30 days, so if the pause plus the migration ran long enough, the TTL expiry and then the DLQ retention window could both have elapsed.

Ten days of pause alone would put them in the DLQ as TTLExpired, so check there with a wider window:

zephyr dlq list --queue <q> --limit 500 --json

and filter for TTLExpired. If they are genuinely not there, the 30-day DLQ retention has passed and they are unrecoverable.

posts.body: Worker RSS climbs from 180 MB to about 1.4 GB over four days, then the supervisor OOM-kills it. Concurrency 25, handlers are short, no obvious accumulation in my own code. Anyone seen this?
